article.overview: A radio frequency spectrum analyser on the Moon measures how much radio power arrives at the surface or in lunar orbit across a range of frequencies, and how that power changes with time. It is used to listen for radio emissions from the Sun, the Milky Way, planets and, at low frequencies, the early Universe, and to measure radio-frequency interference (RFI) from spacecraft and Earth-based transmitters. The lunar far side is of particular interest because the Moon shields an instrument there from most human-made radio noise from Earth. 'Radio frequency spectrum analyser' is a broad class name in the catalogue rather than one standard instrument. This article describes the class and reviews specific instruments that have flown, are planned, or are only proposed. Their specifications are not interchangeable.
article.description: A radio spectrum analyser consists of one or more antennas, a low-noise receiver chain with filters and amplifiers, an analogue-to-digital converter, and a digital processor that computes the power in each frequency channel. The output is usually a power spectral density recorded over time as a dynamic spectrum. Lunar instruments of this kind typically use long dipole or monopole antennas, because the wavelengths involved, from tens of metres near 10 MHz to kilometres at a few hundred kHz, are far larger than any practical receiver housing. A single lunar spectrometer records a local view, and its usefulness grows when several instruments or observing campaigns are combined.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Main applications in the sources reviewed: (1) Radio astronomy below the ionospheric cutoff. Earth's ionosphere blocks most radio waves below roughly 10 to 15 MHz; the ROLSES mission describes its purpose in these terms, noting that radio waves below about 15 MHz cannot be seen from Earth because of the ionospheric cutoff (arXiv:2603.22600). (2) Solar and plasma radio emission. The Chang'e-4 Low-frequency Radio Spectrometer (LFRS) was designed to study solar radio bursts and the local plasma environment across 0.1 to 40 MHz according to the Zhu et al. 2020 preprint (arXiv:2012.04347); the detailed goals should be checked against that preprint. (3) Cosmic dark-ages cosmology. LuSEE-Night and CosmoCube are described for detecting the redshifted 21 cm hydrogen line, a faint signal expected at frequencies below about 50 MHz (arXiv:2407.07173; arXiv:2406.10096). (4) Characterising RFI and the lunar radio environment. The Longjiang-2 team reported RFI below a few MHz under the receiver noise floor and estimated about 80 dB of RFI suppression would be needed at lunar distance from Earth; the 80 dB value is an estimate, not a measurement (arXiv:2212.09590; Yan et al. 2023).
article.operating_principle: Common to the instruments reviewed: (1) Collection. Antennas convert the incident electromagnetic field into a small voltage; dipoles or monopoles several metres long are typical at low MHz frequencies. (2) Conditioning. A low-noise amplifier and band-limiting filters reject out-of-band signals and set the receiver noise floor. The Chang'e-4 LFRS quotes a receiver sensitivity of at most 10 nV/sqrt(Hz) (arXiv:2604.07920, Section II). (3) Digitisation. ROLSES uses a 14-bit ADC at 120 megasamples per second (arXiv:2603.22600). (4) Spectral analysis. A digital processor, usually an FPGA, performs an FFT and averages the results. The ROLSES abstract states an onboard FPGA performs FFT spectral analysis; the CosmoCube testbed uses a 4096-point FFT with 62.5 kHz bins (arXiv:2406.10096, Table 3). (5) Recording and downlink. Time-averaged spectra and, in some missions, raw waveforms are stored and transmitted through a relay or direct link. Calibration, self-generated RFI from spacecraft electronics, and lander-structure effects on antenna patterns all affect the result. The LFRS authors describe intense electromagnetic interference from the lander and its environment that had to be mitigated (arXiv:2012.04347).
article.scientific_importance: Radio emission at the lowest frequencies is reflected or absorbed by Earth's ionosphere before reaching the ground, so the Moon is one of the few places where it can be measured directly. The Chang'e-4 LFRS began observing on 5 January 2019 (arXiv:2604.07920, Section II) and has produced a long record from the far side. A 2026 preprint uses that record to search for periodic signals; identifying and rejecting RFI is central to that analysis (arXiv:2604.07920). Longjiang-2 showed that a spectrometer in lunar orbit could make measurements from 1 to 30 MHz during about a year of operation (Yan et al. 2023). The main uncertainty is how well a single instrument can separate faint cosmic signals from its own and the spacecraft's RFI. Several proposed missions are designed around this problem, but most have not yet demonstrated the required performance on the Moon.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power figure for a radio frequency spectrum analyser. Values below describe named instruments only. Status labels: flown = operated in space or on the Moon; planned = scheduled, operation not confirmed; proposed = design or testbed without a flight receiver. Null means not stated in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: Chang'e-4 Low-frequency Radio Spectrometer (LFRS)
examples.launch_and_operation: Launched December 2018 on Chang'e-4 (arXiv:2012.04347); observations began 5 January 2019 (arXiv:2604.07920, Section II).
examples.receiver_sensitivity: At most 10 nV/sqrt(Hz) (arXiv:2604.07920, Section II). The 2020 abstract gives 1e-18 W m^-2 Hz^-1, described as tentative and following EMI mitigation (arXiv:2012.04347).
examples.antennas: Three orthogonal 5 m dipoles and a 20 cm short antenna (D) for noise mitigation and calibration (arXiv:2604.07920, Section II).
examples.spectral_resolution: At most 10 kHz (low band) and 200 kHz (high band); 2048 channels per science record (arXiv:2604.07920, Section II). Section V.1 gives about 19 kHz, which conflicts with the Section II low-band figure and is unresolved.
examples.unverified_secondary_values: A 2019 EPSC-DPS poster, seen only in a search snippet and not retrieved in full, reports dynamic range of at least 75 dB, data rate up to 5 Mbps and power up to 24 W. These values are unverified.

examples.name: ROLSES on Intuitive Machines IM-1
examples.type: Flown lunar surface radio and plasma wave instrument
examples.launch_and_operation: Operated on the lunar surface near the south pole (Malapert A, about 80 S) on the Odysseus lander under NASA CLPS; observations made during transit and surface operations (arXiv:2603.22600).
examples.antennas: Four 2.5 m radio monopoles, stowed for launch and deployed after landing via a Frangibolt mechanism (arXiv:2603.22600).
examples.onboard_processing: FPGA FFT spectral analysis; outputs are time-averaged spectra and raw waveforms (arXiv:2603.22600).
examples.lander_effects: Abstract describes a tilted landing of Odysseus but does not quantify its effect on ROLSES objectives. A search snippet of the paper says only some objectives were addressed; not confirmed in full text.

examples.name: Longjiang-2 Low Frequency Interferometer and Spectrometer (LFIS)
examples.launch_and_operation: Longjiang-1 and Longjiang-2 launched 21 May 2018 with the Queqiao relay satellite (secondary source). Only Longjiang-2 flew, operating as a single telescope (Yan et al. 2023, secondary summary). Commissioning confirmed reliable operation; about one year of operation; 81 observations near the lunar limb; disposed onto the lunar surface 31 July 2019 (secondary source, Yan et al. 2023).
examples.frequency_source: Yan et al. 2023 as summarised in a secondary search result. The arXiv abstract refers only to frequencies below a few MHz.
examples.rfi_note: RFI below a few MHz reported as smaller than the receiver noise floor. An RFI suppression of about 80 dB is estimated as required at lunar distance (secondary source; an estimate, not a measurement).

examples.name: LuSEE-Night
examples.type: Planned lunar far-side lander radio spectrometer
examples.launch_and_operation: Planned payload on the top deck of the Firefly Blue Ghost Mission 2 lander to the lunar far side. Wikipedia (last edited 29 October 2026) gives a 2027 launch, no landing date and no operational outcome; the schedule is unverified and earlier sources gave different dates.
examples.power_summary: Per the arXiv abstract, a single 7 kWh battery with photovoltaic support must keep the spectrometer powered through two weeks of lunar night. Taken from the abstract summary; verify against the full paper.
examples.operation_summary: Drift-scan observations during the lunar night; data relayed to Earth through an orbital relay during the lunar day. Expected operating life up to two years (Wikipedia).

examples.name: CosmoCube lunar-orbit 21 cm spectrometer
examples.type: Proposed lunar-orbit cubesat spectrometer with laboratory testbed
examples.hardware_status: Engineering testbed on a Xilinx ZCU111 evaluation board. Paper states no receiver has yet been coupled and the RFSoC is not yet fully space-qualified (arXiv:2406.10096, Section 5). Not flight hardware.
examples.dynamic_range_db: About 80 dB, as a requirement or estimate, not measured (arXiv:2406.10096, Sections 2 and 3).

power_w.basis: Vivado-reported in Table 3; whether measured or estimated is not specified

examples.sensitivity_target: 10 mK after about 1000 hours of integration. A target; not demonstrated (arXiv:2406.10096, Section 2).
examples.rfi_treatment: Observations planned during Earth occultation with a shielded zone of about 6,700 km from the lunar centre (Section 2). The 62.5 kHz bin width may be too coarse for narrowband RFI (Section 4.2). No flight RFI mitigation or on-orbit RFI measurement reported.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The dominant dimension of a low-frequency spectrometer is set by its antennas: the Chang'e-4 LFRS uses 5 m dipoles and ROLSES uses 2.5 m monopoles. CosmoCube is a proposed 12U or 16U cubesat; its electronics dimensions are not published in the source reviewed. Dimensions must be determined from the intended measurement band, the antenna pattern required and the mounting constraints of the host spacecraft.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is not published for four of the five examples. Where it is given (none in this set), it applies only to the named instrument and should not be used as a general figure for the class. Mass affects launch, lander capacity and structural design.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power is reported for only some examples and the values are not directly comparable: LuSEE-Night battery sizing for lunar night (abstract summary); CosmoCube Vivado-reported estimate of 5.45 W and 6.1 W for a testbed configuration; an unverified secondary figure of up to 24 W for the Chang'e-4 LFRS.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar radio spectrometer must survive the thermal, radiation and dust environment of its location. It also has specific needs. Shielding from Earth's radio noise: the far side, or lunar orbit during Earth occultation, blocks most terrestrial RFI; CosmoCube plans observations during Earth occultation with a shielded zone of about 6,700 km (arXiv:2406.10096, Section 2). Self-generated RFI: the ROLSES paper expected RFI from its own digital signal processing (search snippet of arXiv:2603.22600). Lander electronics and power converters also contribute. Antenna environment: long antennas must be deployed and kept in a stable configuration, and the LFRS authors describe an intense electromagnetic environment from the lander (arXiv:2012.04347). Power through lunar night: surface instruments that observe through the night need power for about two weeks of darkness, as in the LuSEE-Night design (arXiv:2407.07173). Thermal stability: the CosmoCube testbed showed ±0.2 dB over 5 to 40 degrees C in a laboratory chamber, which is not a demonstration in the lunar thermal environment (arXiv:2406.10096, Section 4.4).
article.limitations: The instrument class has no single specification, so values describe individual instruments only. Most performance values come from papers and preprints rather than in-flight calibration reports reviewed in this run. The LFRS channel-resolution figure is inconsistent between Section II and Section V.1 of arXiv:2604.07920. RFI estimates such as the 80 dB figure are estimates, not measurements. Antenna behaviour on a lander can differ from its ideal pattern, and the sources reviewed do not quantify this for each mission. The LuSEE-Night and CosmoCube sources describe plans and targets, not measured performance.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Surface payloads of this type are delivered as part of a lander's payload complement: integration on Earth, launch, transfer to the Moon, landing, deployment, and connection to the lander's power and data systems. Orbital payloads follow spacecraft integration, launch, cruise and orbit insertion.
transportation_process: Integrate the spectrometer and antennas with the lander or spacecraft on Earth.
Launch on a launch vehicle and transfer to the Moon.
Land or insert into lunar orbit.
Deploy antennas (for surface payloads) and check the instrument in the lunar environment.
Connect to lander or spacecraft power and data systems and begin observations.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: ROLSES was stowed for launch and its four 2.5 m monopoles were released after landing by a Frangibolt mechanism (arXiv:2603.22600). The Chang'e-4 LFRS deployment mechanism is not described in the sources reviewed. LuSEE-Night is a top-deck payload on the Blue Ghost Mission 2 lander (Wikipedia); its deployment is not described in the sources reviewed. Longjiang-2 was a selenocentric orbiter and was disposed of onto the lunar surface at the end of its mission (secondary source).
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Chang'e-4 LFRS on the far-side lander (2019 onward) and ROLSES on IM-1 at the south pole (landing date not given in the sources reviewed) are flown examples of surface instruments. Longjiang-2 is a flown lunar-orbit example.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility claim is made with any named lander or spacecraft beyond what the payload listing for LuSEE-Night on Blue Ghost Mission 2 states. Compatibility for a future spectrometer would need to be assessed against its mass, dimensions, antenna deployment loads, power, thermal and data interfaces, and the verified specification of the host vehicle.

article.historical_significance: Low-frequency radio spectrometers on the Moon are a recent development. The Chang'e-4 LFRS, operating on the far side from January 2019, has produced a long data record and is used in a 2026 search for periodic signals (arXiv:2604.07920). Longjiang-2 was an early demonstration of a lunar-orbit radio spectrometer with reported measurements from 1 to 30 MHz (Yan et al. 2023). ROLSES added a surface instrument at the lunar south pole, a different environment from the far side. LuSEE-Night and CosmoCube are proposed missions intended to build on these results toward cosmological observations.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: LuSEE-Night flight status is not confirmed in the sources reviewed; the Wikipedia page describes planned activities only, and its launch date (2027) conflicts with an earlier late-2026 estimate on the same page. Mass and power are not published for several examples. The Chang'e-4 LFRS channel resolution is inconsistent within arXiv:2604.07920. The Longjiang-2 frequency range is from a secondary summary of Yan et al. 2023; the arXiv abstract did not give it. The 80 dB RFI suppression figure is an estimate. CosmoCube sensitivity (10 mK) and dynamic range (about 80 dB) are design targets, not demonstrated end to end. Imagery was not researched to the required standard in this run; no direct image asset URLs were verified.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No image URLs were verified in this run, so no image objects are included.

data_quality_notes: No direct image asset URLs were verified; image arrays are empty and no images appear in the article.
Chang'e-4 LFRS channel resolution differs between arXiv:2604.07920 Section II (at most 10 kHz low band) and Section V.1 (about 19 kHz).
Chang'e-4 LFRS dynamic range, data rate and power (75 dB, 5 Mbps, 24 W) come from a 2019 EPSC-DPS poster seen only in a search snippet and are unverified.
Longjiang-2 LFIS frequency range (1 to 30 MHz) and the 80 dB RFI estimate come from a secondary summary of Yan et al. 2023; the arXiv abstract was retrieved but does not state them.

LuSEE-Night flight status is unverified. The Blue Ghost Mission 2 Wikipedia page (last edited 29 October 2026) gives a 2027 launch and no outcome, and conflicts internally with an earlier late-2026 estimate.
LuSEE-Night 7 kWh battery figure is taken from an arXiv abstract summary and should be checked against the full paper.
ROLSES lander-limitation statement (only some objectives addressed) is from a search snippet and is not confirmed in the full text.
CosmoCube sensitivity (10 mK) and dynamic range (about 80 dB) are design targets, not demonstrated. Power values are Vivado-reported.
Several PDF documents could not be read as text in this run (binary PDF fetch); HTML or abstract pages were used instead where available.
The Moon-based location and lander compatibility questions are not resolved; no compatibility is asserted beyond the cited payload listings.
